subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which feature is present in a bacterial (prokaryotic) cell?
options: A nucleus enclosing the DNA
Mitochondria
Chloroplasts
A single loop of DNA in the cytoplasm
questions.explain: Bacteria have no nucleus; their genetic material is a single circular DNA loop free in the cytoplasm, sometimes with plasmids.

questions.q: In osmosis, water moves from a region where it is:
options: Less concentrated to more concentrated, using energy
More concentrated (dilute solution) to where it is less concentrated (concentrated solution)
More concentrated to a more concentrated solution against the gradient
Equally concentrated on both sides at all times
questions.explain: Water moves from a dilute solution (high water concentration) to a concentrated solution (low water concentration) across a partially permeable membrane.

questions.q: Why does a small cube of agar absorb a dye faster than a large cube of the same shape?
options: The large cube has a higher surface area to volume ratio
Diffusion does not depend on surface area
The small cube has less surface area in total
The small cube has a higher surface area to volume ratio
questions.explain: A smaller cube has a larger surface area relative to its volume, so substances diffuse in more quickly.

questions.q: A cell appears 40 mm wide under a microscope at a magnification of ×400. What is its actual width?
options: 0.1 mm
0.4 mm
16 mm
100 mm
questions.explain: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 40 ÷ 400 = 0.1 mm.

questions.q: Enzymes are best described as:
options: Sources of energy for cells
Carbohydrates that store energy
Biological catalysts that speed up reactions
Substances used up in reactions
questions.explain: Enzymes are biological catalysts; they speed up reactions and are not used up.

questions.q: An image of a cell is 30 mm long and the magnification is ×1500. What is the actual size?
options: 20 µm
450 µm
questions.explain: Actual = image ÷ magnification = 30 mm ÷ 1500 = 0.02 mm = 20 µm.

questions.q: The part of an enzyme where the substrate fits is called the:
options: Optimum site
Active site
Reaction centre
Lock site
questions.explain: The substrate binds to the active site of the enzyme, which has a complementary shape.

questions.q: Why does a very high or very low pH usually stop an enzyme working?
options: It gives the enzyme more energy
It changes the shape of the active site, denaturing the enzyme
It freezes the enzyme
It turns the enzyme into a product
questions.explain: Extreme pH alters the active site's shape (denaturation) so the substrate no longer fits.

questions.q: A positive Biuret test for protein is shown by a colour change from:
options: Purple to colourless
Blue to purple/lilac
Blue to brick-red
Brown to blue-black
questions.explain: Biuret reagent (blue) turns purple/lilac when protein is present.

questions.q: Which combination of food test and positive result is correct?
options: Biuret solution turns brick-red with protein
Ethanol turns blue-black with lipids
Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black with starch
Benedict's solution turns purple with starch
questions.explain: Iodine solution changes from orange-brown to blue-black in the presence of starch.

questions.q: Enzymes speed up reactions but are not used up themselves. This means an enzyme can:
options: Only be used once and then destroyed
Be reused to catalyse the reaction many times
Only work below 0 °C
Change permanently into the product
questions.explain: As catalysts, enzymes are not used up in the reaction and can be used again and again.

questions.q: Why must a Biuret test for protein be carried out without heating, unlike the Benedict's test?
options: Because heating turns all proteins into sugars
Because protein only forms in the cold
Because the Biuret test gives its colour change at room temperature
Because protein is destroyed by Benedict's solution
questions.explain: The Biuret test produces a purple/lilac colour at room temperature, so heating is not required (unlike Benedict's test for sugars).

questions.q: Why does an electron microscope allow us to see more detail than a light microscope?
options: It has a much higher magnification and resolution
It uses a brighter light source
It magnifies but has lower resolution
It only works on living cells
questions.explain: Electron microscopes have far higher magnification and resolution, revealing sub-cellular structures.

questions.q: A cell is 0.05 mm wide. What is this in micrometres (µm)?
options: 500 µm
5 µm
50 µm

questions.q: Which of these is the smallest and would need the highest magnification to be seen?
options: A bacterium
A red blood cell
A cheek cell
A mitochondrion
questions.explain: A mitochondrion is a sub-cellular organelle and is smaller than a whole bacterium or animal cell.

questions.q: Active transport differs from diffusion because it:
options: Does not require a cell membrane
Moves substances down the concentration gradient
Requires energy from respiration to move substances against the gradient
Only moves water molecules
questions.explain: Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient and needs energy (ATP) from respiration.

questions.q: Osmosis is the movement of:
options: Water from a concentrated to a dilute solution
Particles from high to low concentration using ATP
Water from a dilute to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
Any dissolved solute across a membrane
questions.explain: Osmosis is the diffusion of water only, from a dilute (high water) to a more concentrated (low water) solution through a partially permeable membrane.

questions.q: What is the role of the permanent vacuole in a plant cell?
options: Controls cell division
Contains cell sap to keep the cell turgid (firm)
Site of respiration
Makes proteins
questions.explain: The vacuole is filled with cell sap and helps keep the plant cell rigid and supported.

questions.q: The 'lock and key' model explains that an enzyme:
options: Is destroyed after each reaction
Provides energy to the substrate
Works on any substrate
Has an active site with a specific shape that fits a particular substrate
questions.explain: The active site has a complementary shape to its specific substrate, like a key fitting a lock.

questions.q: Why is glucose absorbed from the small intestine into the blood sometimes by active transport?
options: Glucose is always at a higher concentration in the gut
To absorb glucose even when its concentration is higher in the blood than the gut
Glucose cannot diffuse at all
To move water into the blood
questions.explain: Active transport allows glucose to be absorbed against the gradient when blood glucose is higher than in the gut.

questions.q: When an enzyme is denatured, what has happened to its active site?
options: It has become larger to fit more substrate
It has been killed and is now dead
It has joined permanently with the product
It has changed shape so the substrate no longer fits
questions.explain: Denaturing changes the shape of the active site so the substrate can no longer fit; the enzyme is not 'killed' as it was never alive.

questions.q: In an osmosis experiment, why should the potato chips be dried with a paper towel before being reweighed?
options: To make the chips heavier
To stop osmosis happening
To kill the cells before weighing
To remove surface liquid so only the change inside the chip is measured
questions.explain: Drying removes excess surface solution so the recorded mass reflects water moving in or out of the cells, not liquid clinging to the surface.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9–1) Biology (1BI0) specification; Key Concepts In Biology
